Adapters.description:
`[adapters]` — which implementation satisfies each contract.

A plain map rather than a struct with a field per contract: the contract set
is declared once in `crate::adapter::CONTRACTS`, and a struct here would be
a second copy of it that drifts the first time one is added.

Advise.description:
`[advise]` — is advisory review part of this product's procedure.

On by default, and **off by declaration**: setting `enabled = false` is the
escape hatch (principle 3), usable at any point in a product's life, not a
choice that has to be made at `fid new`. It lives in `fiducial.toml` because
a switch that exists only in someone's shell or a CI dashboard cannot be
reviewed, reverted or known about by an agent (principle 4).

It switches the *asking* off and nothing else. `fid derive`, `fid doctor`
and the guard never read it, so it cannot change a build — the property
`tests/determinism.rs` holds for the key holds for this too.

enabled.description:
Absent means on: a product that predates this block is not silently
opted out of the procedure.

Ai.description:
`[ai]` — what an AI gateway needs that nothing can derive.

The contract targets a gateway rather than a model vendor, so the vendor
axis (`[adapters] ai`) and the *model* axis are different facts: switching
from Claude to GPT is a one-line change here and no adapter change at all.
That is the whole point of the gateway decision, and it only holds if the
model is a declaration.

So it is declared once here and derived into the generated factory, where
`fid derive --check` gates it like every other derived fact. A per-call
`request.model` still wins — an agent that classifies with a small model
and answers with a large one is a normal agent, and forcing it to build a
second adapter would make this declaration a lie rather than a default.

base_url.description:
The OpenAI-compatible endpoint, for `ai = "ollama"`: a plain-http URL
ending in `/v1`. Empty means the Compose service,
`http://ollama:11434/v1`.

model.description:
Gateway model id, e.g. `anthropic/claude-opus-5`.

Deliberately **not defaulted**. Any default the platform picked would
be a vendor choice made on the product's behalf, and would age into a
model that no longer exists — silently, since a gateway reports an
unknown model at the first call rather than at deploy.

App.description:
One app's choices. Every field is optional: an app declares only what it
chooses, and a missing field is the capability's own default.

api.description: The backend this app talks to, when it is not its own: `hono`.

editor.description: The content editor for this app's files: `keystatic`, `tina`.

shell.description: Zero or more native shells that wrap the built app.

Brand.description:
`[brand]` — the one declaration every brand-derived artifact reads.

Legal name, trading name, domain and contact email have no platform
default — they are facts about one product, not a decision this platform
can make on a product's behalf. The `brand` capability seeds them as
placeholder text precisely so `is_empty` is false and the pipeline it
installs does not fail on the very next `fid derive`; `validate` then
catches whichever placeholder a product forgot to replace.

favicon.description:
A product-supplied favicon, relative to the product root.

The generated favicon is initials on a coloured square, which is the
right default and the wrong answer for any product that has an actual
mark. Without this, the only ways out are hand-editing a derived file —
which `fid derive --check` correctly fails — or dropping `favicon.svg`
from the pipeline's outputs, which silently loses the artifact.

So this is the documented override that MISSION.md principle 3 requires:
the file stays derived, `--check` still guards it, and the declaration
says where its content comes from. The file is copied verbatim; nothing
here parses or rewrites SVG.

platform_credit.description:
Whether the product's footer credits Fiducial.

**Opt-in, and false by default.** A credit line is a sentence printed on
somebody else's page, under their brand, to their readers. A platform
that adds one unless you find the switch has made a claim on a surface
it does not own, and the products most likely to never notice are
exactly the ones — a client site, a white-label build — where it is
least appropriate. Opting in costs one line; opting out of something you
never knew was there costs finding out from the client.

Always serialized rather than hidden when false, so the flag is
discoverable by reading `fiducial.toml` instead of by reading this
struct (MISSION.md 4: everything explicit, in git).

short_name.description:
Home-screen label. Falls back to `trading_name`.

`site.webmanifest` used to put the trading name in both `name` and
`short_name`, which defeats the point of the field: `short_name` is what
a phone prints under an icon, in about twelve characters, and "Fire
Outreach Network" is not that. A product with a short name already
declares nothing here and loses nothing.

ComposeService.description: One extra service in a self-hosted product's Compose file.

environment.description: Plain values only. A secret is named in `secrets` and set in `.env`.

healthcheck.description: A shell command; exit 0 is healthy.

secrets.description: Names of secrets, written as `${NAME}`, never as a value.

volumes.description: `name:/path` is a named volume; `./dir:/path` is a bind mount.

Deploy.description:
`[deploy]` — what a deploy config needs that `[adapters]` cannot imply.

The split is the whole point. Which bindings a Worker needs **is** derivable
— `[adapters]` already says `database = "d1"`, and the `D1Database` adapter
already reads a fixed `env.DB`. What is not derivable is everything only the
Cloudflare account knows: the database's id, the bucket's name, the route.
Those live here; the bindings are generated around them.

api_prefix.description:
The path prefix Caddy proxies to the server when `static_dir` is set.
Defaults to `/api`.

assets_binding.description: The binding the Worker reads those assets through.

assets_directory.description:
Where the adapter writes the static assets it wants served.

Only read for `shape = "sveltekit"` and `"nextjs"`, and defaulted to the adapter's own
output directory — a product that has not moved it declares nothing.

compatibility_date.description:
Wrangler `compatibility_date`. Pinned, never "today": a date that moves
changes runtime behaviour under a product that did not ask it to.

crons.description:
Cron expressions this Worker is triggered on, e.g. `["0 2 * * *"]`.

Emitted as `triggers.crons` in the derived wrangler config. The
expressions are Cloudflare's cron syntax (UTC), and each one becomes a
scheduled trigger that runs the Worker's `scheduled` handler.

Because cron schedules are facts about the product — not vendor account
data — they belong here rather than in a hand-edited config section.

custom_domain.description:
Whether `route` is a **custom domain** rather than a zone route.

The distinction is not cosmetic, and getting it wrong fails the deploy
rather than producing something subtly off:

- A **zone route** (`"route": "example.com/*"`) matches traffic that
  already arrives at Cloudflare. It needs a proxied DNS record for that
  hostname to exist, and `wrangler deploy` will not create one. On a
  registrar's parked apex it fails with `code: 100117`.
- A **custom domain** (`"routes": [{ "pattern": …, "custom_domain":
  true }]`) makes Cloudflare create the DNS record and issue the
  certificate itself.

For a product whose Worker *is* the site — `sveltekit` and `nextjs` —
the custom domain is almost always what is meant, and it was
inexpressible here until this field existed. `aleksa.works` therefore
hand-edited the derived `wrangler.jsonc`, which is the single thing this
capability exists to prevent.

Left `false` so an existing product's generated config does not change
shape under it: a zone route is what `route` has always meant.

d1_database_id.description: D1 database id — from `wrangler d1 create`. Only the account knows it.

d1_database_name.description: D1 database name, defaulting to the product name.

durable_objects.description:
Durable Object classes this Worker exports and binds. Like KV, a fact
about the product's own Worker rather than a vendor choice. The class
must be exported from `main` (for the Next.js shape, a one-line
re-export beside OpenNext's handler). Declared as SQLite-backed, the
only kind the free plan allows.

host.description:
The hostname a self-hosted product answers on (`deploy = "compose"`):
a LAN name such as `building.local`, or a public domain. Read only by
`fid-compose`.

kv_namespaces.description:
KV namespaces this product binds that no `[adapters]` contract covers.

The derived bindings come from vendor selections, which is right for
the contracts that exist — but a product's own KV namespace is not a
vendor choice, it is a fact about its account. One product's live
signup counter is written by an external script into a namespace whose
id must survive every migration; there was nowhere to declare that, so
its config could not be derived at all.

main.description: Worker entrypoint, relative to the worker app.

name.description: Worker name. Defaults to `<product>-worker` when left empty.

observability.description: Whether to turn on Workers observability.

proxy.description:
Which service Caddy proxies to (`deploy = "compose"`). Defaults to the
first app of the first host node, or `server` with no topology.

proxy_port.description: The port that service listens on. Defaults to 8080.

r2_bucket_name.description: R2 bucket name — from `wrangler r2 bucket create`.

registry.description: Where the server image is pushed and pulled (`deploy = "compose"`).

route.description:
Route or custom domain this Worker answers on. Optional: a Worker on
its `workers.dev` subdomain declares none.

run_worker_first.description:
Paths that run the Worker **before** the static assets are consulted
(`["/api/*"]`). A static site served as Workers Static Assets answers
every request from files and wakes no code; a site with one dynamic
route (a counter, a form handler) names that route here and keeps every
other request free. Needs a Worker (`main`), since a path with nothing to
run is a typo, not a setting.

secrets.description:
Secret names this Worker reads that no `[adapters]` selection implies.

Names only, never values. Each name appears in the generated
`wrangler secret put` comment block so a deployer knows what to set.
Values must never enter a file in the repository.

Adapter-implied secrets (`TURNSTILE_SECRET_KEY`, `RESEND_API_KEY`, …)
are already added automatically; list only secrets the product's own
code reads that nothing else declares.

services.description:
Services this product runs that nothing else declares: a database, a
cache, a worker (`deploy = "compose"`). Apps, the broker and Ollama are
derived and are not listed here.

shape.description:
What is being deployed — and it is not the same artifact in both cases.

`worker` (the default) is a standalone Worker at `apps/worker/`, whose
entrypoint is a source file this repository wrote.

`sveltekit` is a SvelteKit app where **`apps/web` is the Worker**, by
way of `@sveltejs/adapter-cloudflare`: the entrypoint and the static
assets are both *build output*, and the config lives at the product
root because that is where the adapter looks for it.

Without this, `fid add deploy` on a SvelteKit product wrote an
`apps/worker/wrangler.toml` describing nothing the product runs, while
the real config stayed untracked — worse than not running it, and the
reason one product declared `[adapters] deploy = "cloudflare"` and
deliberately did not install this capability.

static_dir.description:
A static export Caddy serves (`deploy = "compose"`): the web app's build
directory, relative to the product root, e.g. `apps/web/out`. Built with
`STATIC_EXPORT=1` (`pnpm build:static`). With it, `proxy` receives only
`api_prefix/*`; without it, `proxy` receives everything.

tls.description:
How Caddy gets its certificate (`deploy = "compose"`): `internal` (its
own CA, for a LAN name, the default) or `acme` (a public domain).

vars.description:
Plain environment variables. Values are **not** secrets — those are
named in a comment and set with `wrangler secret put`, never written
into a file in the repository.

workers_dev.description:
Whether the Worker also answers on its `workers.dev` subdomain.

`None` means "do not write the field", which is not the same as `false`:
wrangler's own default is on when no route is declared and **off when
one is**, so a product that declares a route silently loses the URL it
has been checking deploys against. That happened on the first
`aleksa.works` custom-domain deploy and took the preview URL down with
it, which is why this is declarable at all rather than left to the
default.

Design.description:
`[design]` — registries the product's components come from.

```toml
[design.registries]
"@acme" = "https://acme.example/r/{name}.json"
```

shadcn resolves `npx shadcn add @acme/button` through the `registries` map
in `components.json`. That file is a copy of this declaration, rewritten by
`fid derive`, so the list a product installs from is written once.

github.description:
`owner/repo` of the public GitHub repository this product is pushed to.

shadcn reads a repository with a root `registry.json` as a registry
(`npx shadcn add owner/repo/button`), with nothing to host or build. When
this is declared, the registry's items name each other that way instead
of through an `@namespace` the installing product would have to configure.

DurableObject.description: One Durable Object binding: the name the Worker reads, and the class it is.

binding.description: The binding name in the Worker, e.g. `REALTIME`.

Freshness.description:
`[freshness]` — how this repository stops a stale artifact reaching `main`.

`fid dash` used to equate "gated" with "a workflow runs `fid derive
--check`", and reported *this* repository as ungated while seven gates ran
on every commit. The reason is in `fiducial.toml`: the protocol vectors and
the terminal captures are gated by Rust tests on purpose, because a gate
that runs through the tool it gates is blind exactly where it matters.

That is a judgment, so it is declared rather than guessed. `fid derive
--check` stays recognised without being listed — it is the default for a
scaffolded product, and requiring every product to restate it would be the
second declaration this block exists to avoid.

gates.description:
Commands that gate a generated artifact, matched as substrings against
each workflow's text.

Guard.description: Guard configuration — what `fid guard-check` enforces in this product.

rules.description: Named rule sets that are active.

I18n.description:
`[i18n]` — the locales this product ships.

Declared rather than inferred. `default` is **not** `locales[0]`: which
language a product falls back to is a decision, and inferring it from list
order is exactly the kind of implicit fact this platform exists to delete.

Empty `locales` means the product is not localized. That is a valid state
for a CLI or a firmware image, and `fid new --locales none` asks for it — but
`fid new` seeds the `i18n` capability's own locales otherwise, because a product that can be
built monolingual will be, and principle 1c says monolingual is a state you
pass through before the first commit.

messages_dir.description:
Directory holding `<locale>.json`, relative to the product root.

`serde(default)` fills this when *reading*; without the matching skip it
round-tripped a `Default::default()` value back out as `""`, which then
failed to resolve on the next read.

same.description:
Keys whose value is the same in every locale on purpose — a product
name, "Wi-Fi". Any other value identical to the default locale's is
untranslated, and `fid derive --check` refuses it.

Identity.description:
`[identity]` — what grant storage cannot derive from the model.

The grants table's *shape* follows from the identity model: its `CHECK`
constraints are the `Principal`, `Resource` and `Role` variants. Three
things do not follow from it, and live here.

**The dialect is derived, not declared** — by default. `[adapters]
database` already names the vendor, and the vendor implies the dialect:
`d1` is SQLite, `supabase`/`neon`/`postgres` are Postgres. Declaring it
again would be the copy that goes wrong, so `dialect` is an *override* for
the case the platform cannot see (a product pointing `none` at a real
database of its own).

audit.description:
Derive an append-only log of authorization decisions.

Off by default. An audit log is a write on every decision and a
retention obligation on every row, so it is a choice a product makes
rather than something it acquires by installing identity.

It arrives as `migrations/0002_audit.sql` — a *second* migration, not
an edit to the first. Editing an applied migration is the one thing the
migration runner refuses outright, and the generator does not get an
exemption from the rule it generates for.

current_user_sql.description:
The SQL expression yielding the current user's id, for RLS.

Defaults to Supabase's `auth.uid()`. A product connecting with a
per-request role instead would use something like
`current_setting('app.user_id', true)`. Normalized to this platform's
hex form by the generator, because `auth.uid()` returns a hyphenated
UUID and `principal_id` holds 32 hex characters.

dialect.description:
`sqlite` | `postgres`. Empty means "derive it from `[adapters]
database`", which is the normal case.

rls.description:
Generate row-level security policies on the grants table.

Postgres only — SQLite has no RLS. Off by default: a policy that
cannot identify the current user locks the table rather than
protecting it, and whether the database *can* identify them depends on
how the product connects (see `current_user_sql`).

storage.description:
Where the permission rows live: `sql` (the default) or `none`.

`fid add identity` used to install the *rule* and the *storage*
together. A product that wants `can()` and seeds its grants from config
or `MemoryGrantStore` still got a migration it will never apply and a
generated module it will never import.

`none` is this platform's existing word for "wired in, reported, does
nothing" — see the `NONE` adapter, which is a real implementation
rather than a placeholder. Splitting identity into two capabilities was
the alternative, and is more surface for the same result.

table.description: Table holding the permission rows. Defaults to `grants`.

KvNamespace.description: One KV namespace binding: the name the Worker reads, and the account's id.

binding.description: The binding name in the Worker, e.g. `SPOTS`.

id.description:
The namespace id from `wrangler kv namespace create`. Account-specific,
and **load-bearing**: point a deploy at a different id and the data is
silently gone rather than missing.

Legal.description:
`[legal]` — what the legal pipeline needs that `[brand]` cannot imply.

Jurisdiction affects which pages are generated and which clauses are
included. Cookie categories name every tracking purpose the product
declares. `"necessary"` is always included regardless of what the product
lists — it is not a choice.

The `legal` pipeline depends on both `[brand]` (for the entity name, domain,
and contact) and `[i18n]` (for the locale set). Neither dependency is
restated here: they are declared once in their own blocks.

cookie_categories.description: Tracking purposes declared. `"necessary"` is always present.

data_protection_email.description: Email address for data protection enquiries. Appears in every page.

jurisdiction.description:
`EU` | `US` | `UK` | `RS` | `other`. Affects which pages are generated
and which compliance checklist items appear.

last_updated.description:
The date these pages were last reviewed by a person, `YYYY-MM-DD`.

Declared rather than stamped at derive time on purpose. A generated
timestamp would change on every `fid derive` — which breaks
`--check` — and, worse, it would say "reviewed today" about a page
nobody has read since it was scaffolded. This is a human fact, so a
human types it. Omitted, the pages say so out loud.

postal_address.description:
Postal address of the controller. GDPR Art. 13(1)(a) asks for the
controller's identity and contact details; an email alone is thin.

registration_number.description:
Statutory identifiers for the entity, shown on the pages that need them.

Serbia's Zakon o elektronskoj trgovini requires a trader to publish its
registration and tax numbers; the EU e-Commerce Directive asks for the
equivalent. An unincorporated project has neither, and omitting them is
correct in that case — inventing them is not.

name.description: Snake-case product identifier; also used as the crate/package name prefix.

Security.description:
`[security]` — the choices the response headers leave open.

The headers themselves are not declared here: they are one table in the
platform (`security.rs`), derived into every framework's file by
`fid-security`. What a product may choose is the one thing that is a decision
rather than a fact.

hsts_preload.description:
Add `preload` to `Strict-Transport-Security`. Off unless declared: it is
a willingness to be submitted at hstspreload.org, which is slow to undo
(`docs/specs/2026-09-20-hsts-preload.md`).

Skills.description:
`[skills]` — the agents this product's skills are linked for.

Skills live once in `.agents/skills/`, the directory the open `skills` CLI
treats as shared and that Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, OpenCode,
Amp and others read directly. An agent with a directory of its own (Claude
Code reads `.claude/skills/`) gets a link to that copy. The default covers
both groups; list the agents the team actually uses to add or drop links.

Spine.description:
Whether this product uses the L0 Rust spine (fiducial-core etc.).
Pure web products may leave this false.

SystemOne.description:
`[systemOne]` — facts for the typed-decision contract.

Unlike [`Ai`], `model` here is **optional**, and the difference is not an
oversight. `[ai] model` has no safe default because any model the platform
picked would be a vendor choice made for the product, and would age into an
id that no longer exists. The decision vendors publish a *tracking alias* —
`~typesafe/jev-latest` through the gateway, `jev-latest` direct — which by
definition names the current model, so defaulting to it neither picks a
version nor rots. Declaring `model` pins a version instead, which is what a
product wants once an answer distribution matters to it.

model.description:
Decision model id, e.g. `typesafe/jev-1.13`. Empty means the vendor's
tracking alias.

advise.description: `[advise]` — whether advisory review is part of this product's procedure.

ai.description: `[ai]` — the model this product talks to, and how it identifies itself.

apps.description: `[apps.<name>]` — what each app is built with (`crate::apps`).

brand.description:
Skipped when the product declares no brand, so a product that has not
added the `brand` capability carries no empty `[brand]` block.

deploy.description: `[deploy]` — the facts a deploy target needs that nothing can derive.

design.description: `[design]` — the shadcn registries this product installs from.

i18n.description:
Skipped when the product is not localized, so a non-localized product's
`fiducial.toml` carries no empty `[i18n]` block.

identity.description: `[identity]` — where this product keeps its permission rows.

legal.description:
`[legal]` — jurisdiction and cookie declarations for the legal pipeline.

Skipped when the product declares no legal facts, so a product that has
not added the `legal` capability carries no empty `[legal]` block.

security.description: `[security]` — the one choice the response headers leave open.

skills.description: `[skills]` — which agents the platform installs and links skills for.

systemOne.description: `[systemOne]` — the decision model this product asks typed questions of.
